三味線源自中國三弦，約15世紀、室町末期傳至沖繩，形成琉球三線，再傳日本本土，逐: The shamisen derives from the Chinese sanxian, which reached Okinawa around the fifteenth century, at the end of the Muromachi period, and became the Ryukyuan sanshin; it then reached the Japanese mainland, gradually took shape and gave rise to schools such as gidayū and Tsugaru. Early bodies used snakeskin, later dog or cat skin for religious reasons, and from the mid-2000s synthetic skins have become more common. In recent years the Tsugaru shamisen has been used in jazz and rock, and electrified versions with pickups have appeared.

The body is covered with skin, the neck has no frets, and the lowest string is deliberately set low, producing a buzzing tone close to the sitar's. Because the chūzao has a longer fingerboard, its range is higher than the hosozao's and its timbre broader and softer; the Heike shamisen has a shorter neck and a higher range. Volume can be adjusted by the height of the bridge: the higher the bridge, the greater the volume, but fast technique is harder to control; the futozao and the Tsugaru shamisen use thicker necks, are plucked harder and have a more percussive timbre.
三味線為日本弦鳴樂器，常見於傳統劇場與說唱音樂伴奏：長唄三味線用於歌舞伎音樂，義: The shamisen is a Japanese chordophone, commonly heard accompanying traditional theatre and narrative music: the nagauta shamisen in kabuki music, the gidayū shamisen in jōruri and bunraku, and the chūzao types in jiuta, tokiwazu and kiyomoto. It is also used in folk song, where the Tsugaru shamisen accompanies Tsugaru folk songs, and being more open it has entered modern genres such as jazz and rock. It is played by plucking the three strings with a plectrum, the body resonating through its skin, and it can produce timbres ranging from the nimble thin-necked to the full thick-necked.

The neck is wooden — rosewood or sandalwood on fine instruments, padauk on cheap ones — and is usually joined in three sections. The strings are traditionally silk, with nylon also seen; the Heike shamisen uses steel strings. The bridge may be bamboo, ivory, cow bone, water-buffalo horn, rosewood or plastic; plectra are wood, plastic or ivory, often decorated with tortoiseshell. The tuning pegs are traditionally ivory, now mostly wood or plastic.

The shamisen is a traditional Japanese plucked instrument that derives from the Chinese sanxian and took shape after passing through the Ryukyuan sanshin to the Japanese mainland; it is a chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 321.312-6. It consists of a neck, a body and three strings, the body square and covered front and back with skin, the neck without frets; it is played with a ginkgo-shaped plectrum, the body resting on the right thigh. By musical type it divides into hosozao (thin neck), chūzao (middle neck) and futozao (thick neck), and it is commonly heard accompanying kabuki, bunraku, jōruri, jiuta, folk song and Tsugaru folk song.

演奏時將琴身靠在右大腿，左手按弦，右手以撥子撥擊發聲。傳統多採跪坐，現代也可坐椅: In playing, the body rests on the right thigh, the left hand stops the strings and the right hand plucks with a plectrum. Traditionally the player kneels, though a chair may be used today. The neck has no frets, so a beginner must develop a sense of position in the left hand, and may wind cloth around the left hand to help it slide. The three strings, from thick to thin, are the first, second and third, usually tuned to honchōshi, though niaigari or san-sagari can be used; the strings slacken easily during playing and need tuning at any time. The lowest string is deliberately set low to produce a buzz, one of the instrument's basic sounding features.
